title: Boss: five ways to find a thing
brief:
One test, five assertions, and **five different locator strategies** - one each. No starter code.

On the products page, prove that:

1. the **All Products** heading is visible — by *role*
2. the search box is visible — by *placeholder*
3. **Blue Top** is on the page — by *text*
4. there are exactly **8** product cards — by *CSS class*
5. the **third** card is the *Sleeveless Dress* — by *position*, chained onto the CSS locator

For 5, `.nth(2)` is the third card (counting starts at zero) and `to_contain_text` is friendlier than `to_have_text`, because the card also holds a price.

This is the zone's whole toolkit in one function. A reviewer would want each line to use the *simplest* address that could work.
solution:
from playwright.sync_api import Page, expect


def test_the_products_page_shows_the_catalogue(page: Page):
    page.goto("https://automationexercise.com/products")

    # 1. by role
    expect(page.get_by_role("heading", name="All Products")).to_be_visible()

    # 2. by placeholder
    expect(page.get_by_placeholder("Search Product")).to_be_visible()

    # 3. by text
    expect(page.get_by_text("Blue Top")).to_be_visible()

    # 4. by CSS class
    cards = page.locator(".productinfo")
    expect(cards).to_have_count(8)

    # 5. by position, chained onto the CSS locator
    expect(cards.nth(2)).to_contain_text("Sleeveless Dress")

checks.name: role
checks.label: You used a role locator
checks.feedback: No get_by_role in the run. The heading is the one to use it on: get_by_role("heading", name="All Products").

checks.name: placeholder
checks.label: You used a placeholder locator
checks.feedback: No get_by_placeholder in the run. The search box has no label, so its grey hint text is the best handle it has: get_by_placeholder("Search Product").

checks.name: text
checks.label: You used a text locator
checks.feedback: No get_by_text in the run. get_by_text("Blue Top") matches the smallest element containing that text - the product name itself.

checks.name: css
checks.label: You used a CSS locator
checks.feedback: No CSS locator in the run. The product cards have no role and no unique text, which is exactly the case CSS is for: locator(".productinfo").

checks.name: nth
checks.label: You picked one card by position
checks.feedback: No .nth() in the run. Position is the right tool here because 'the third card' is genuinely what the requirement says.

checks.name: to_be_visible
checks.label: Three visibility assertions
checks.feedback: I counted fewer than three to_be_visible checks. If one of your assertions failed, the ones below it never ran - fix the first failure and run again.

checks.name: to_contain_text
checks.label: You check the third card's name
checks.feedback: No to_contain_text check ran. to_have_text would fail here: the card holds the price as well as the name, and to_have_text wants the whole string.

hints.label: Nudge
hints.text: Five assertions, five different locator methods: get_by_role, get_by_placeholder, get_by_text, locator, and .nth() chained onto the last one.

hints.label: Strategy
hints.text: Give the CSS locator a name - cards = page.locator(".productinfo") - and reuse it for both the count and the .nth(2) check. A locator is just an address, so holding on to one costs nothing.

reveal:
The Locator Forest is cleared.

The habit worth taking out of it: **pick the address that describes what the thing is, not where it happens to sit.** Reach down the priority list only when the level above genuinely cannot express what you mean, and leave a note when you do.

Next: **Assertion Ridge**, where you stop finding elements and start making promises about them - and find out why `expect()` waits and `assert` does not.
